attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Keeps 'reaching the point' and 'getting in the way', and marks 'mediocre' as his own judgment. Leaving out the investment-appetite clause is fine because it is evaluative.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary and fair: material restriction of progress, not a permanent ceiling. Requiring more than a change in cooling equipment matches 'progressing much further'. The evaluator picked the Jan–Apr 2024 window, which is reasonable for a present-tense claim.

evidence.note: Schneider Electric's own disclosure, dated March 2024. It says racks above 30kW need new cooling and calls liquid cooling feasible. The contract says a required change in cooling does not meet the support bar, so this neither supports nor refutes a material limit on progress.
CBRE data on 2023: power availability shaped where data centers were built. This is a different period, covers the wider data-center market, and does not measure any limit on AI progress.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows cooling and power pressures, with liquid cooling offered as a workable fix. The contract says that alone is not enough to show physics materially restricting further AI progress. Nothing in the packet shows power and cooling were not constraints either. The 'mediocre' judgment is subjective and not scored. Neither condition is met, so the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: 'I fear' hedges only the hype-cycle clause. The first clause (the AI boom drove the best Q1 in 5 years) is stated firmly. Setting the whole claim's modality to 'may' overstates the hedge, but the contract correctly scores only the firm factual clause.

contract.note: Reading 'driven' as a material contributor and 'global markets' as a broad worldwide aggregate is an ordinary reading of the words. Leaving the feared hype cycle unscored is correct.

evidence.note: XPS commentary from April 2024. It says global equities had their best Q1 since 2019, sparked by an AI boom alongside US economic resilience. It is a secondary summary, but covers both the ranking and AI's contribution.

FT reporting, republished by the Irish Times in March 2024. It ties the strong Q1 to AI enthusiasm and also credits risk appetite, disinflation and economic resilience. That does not rule out a material AI contribution; it only argues against AI being the sole cause.

reviews.rationale: Contemporaneous reporting puts Q1 2024 as global equities' best first quarter since 2019 and names the AI boom as a catalyst. That meets the contract's material-contributor standard. Competing explanations show AI was not the only driver but do not rule out a material contribution. The feared hype cycle is not scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Firm 'will' with two antecedents, failed adoption at scale and a market turn, both kept. No horizon was stated. The 'tens of thousands' threshold is kept.

contract.note: Setting 20,000 as the floor for 'tens of thousands' and requiring the cuts to be caused by the market turn are fair readings. Limiting the count to the AI and cloud industry is an evaluator boundary the speaker did not state, but the text implies it. Requiring a completed episode before a low count can falsify the forecast is appropriate.

evidence.note: Census working paper on Nov 2025–Jan 2026 data, available before the cutoff. It shows limited, uneven AI adoption and rare AI-related job cuts. That bears on the adoption antecedent but does not show a market turn.

Amazon's own disclosure of about 14,000 job cuts in Oct 2025. Amazon attributes them to reducing bureaucracy while the business is performing well, not to failed AI adoption followed by a market turn. They do not qualify.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast with no deadline. The packet does not show the antecedent (failed core adoption followed by a market turn), and no 20,000 attributable job cuts are documented. With the antecedent unknown and no conclusive event, the forecast cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post. 'As I've discussed before' points to his earlier writing, but he still endorses the claim here.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'many businesses' scope, the 'only way' claim that more compute is the sole fix, and the clause about a resource AI is destroying. The proposition is a mix of observation and causal claims; calling it causal is acceptable.

contract.note: Reading 'more compute power' as more model-processing capacity is an ordinary reading. 'Only way' is absolute, so one demonstrated alternative can refute it. It is ambiguous whether the 'dwindling resource' means data or compute, and the contract flags this.

evidence.note: ITI paper, July 2023, before the post. It improved truthfulness with near-zero added compute and can be built into an existing model's bias terms. That is an alternative to more compute, though tested on one benchmark only.

January 2024 study finding hallucinations in 69–88% of verifiable legal queries, which supports material risk in a consequential business use. It does not count affected businesses or address the resource clause.

reviews.rationale: Holds: the hallucination-risk clause is supported for consequential uses such as legal work. Fails: the claim that more compute is the only way to reduce hallucinations is contradicted by an earlier method that cut them with near-zero added compute. Unsettled: no evidence defines or measures the resource AI is said to be destroying.
